h1: Moving from brewer to brewery sales
title: Moving from Brewer to Brewery Sales | Craft Beer School
desc: What brewers bring to brewery sales, what they have to learn about selling and how to decide whether leaving the brewhouse is the right move.
teaser: Brewers know the beer better than anyone in sales. Selling it is a separate skill.
standfirst: Some brewers move into sales because they want daylight hours, more people contact or a different career path. They carry real advantages into the role. They also have to learn targets, negotiation and the patience of a territory plan.
sections: Brewers bring credibility no training can buy

When a brewer walks into a bar, the conversation changes. The bar manager knows they are talking to someone who made the beer, who can explain why it tastes the way it does and who can fix a problem rather than pass it on. That credibility is the brewer's biggest advantage in sales.

Brewers can also train outlet staff properly, describe styles accurately and diagnose dispense problems on the spot. A sales team with an ex-brewer in it tends to handle quality complaints better. Our guide on brewery sales careers lays out what the role usually involves day to day.
Selling is a different job, not an easier one

Brewers often underestimate this. Sales means rejection, sometimes several times a day. It means targets for volume and new outlets, chasing payments and spending hours in traffic between visits. It means negotiating listings, menu placement and support with owners who have three other breweries asking for the same tap.

The work rewards persistence and relationship building more than technical depth. If you enjoy the brewhouse because it is quiet and predictable, think carefully. If you enjoy talking about beer with anyone who will listen, sales may suit you well.

Brewers think in hectolitres and recipes. Outlet owners think in margin per pour, stock turn and footfall. To sell well, you need to understand their numbers. A 50 litre keg holds a fixed number of pours depending on glass size and how much is lost to foam and line cleaning. An owner wants to know how fast that keg will sell and what they make on it.

Learn to talk in those terms. Show how a beer will move, how you will help train staff and what happens if a keg goes wrong. That is a sales conversation. Explaining your hop schedule usually is not.

Most beer complaints in outlets come from the dispense system rather than the brewery. Common causes include dirty lines, wrong gas pressure, warm coolers or old kegs. Draught quality guidance commonly recommends cleaning lines at least every two weeks and holding beer cold, often around 2 to 4 °C.

A brewer turned sales rep can spot these quickly. A dirty line gives lactic sourness or a buttery note. Low pressure gives flat beer. Warm beer foams. Being able to say "the beer is fine, the line needs cleaning, here is how" keeps the account and protects the brand.
Regulation shapes what you can sell

As a brewer you met excise in the form of records and inspections. In sales, it shapes your daily work. Alcohol in India is regulated mostly by states. Outlet licences, pricing, distribution routes and promotions all vary by state and change through notifications.

You will need to know the rules in your territory and work with distributors who hold the right licences. When unsure, ask the regulatory team. It is not something to improvise in front of a customer.

Moving to sales can widen your career. Sales experience combined with brewing knowledge is a strong base for roles in brand management, trade marketing, general management or running your own brewery one day. Many founders say the hardest part of their business was selling the beer, not making it. Our guide on leaving a brewer job to start your own brewery picks up that thread.

On the other hand, your hands-on brewing skills will fade if you are away for years. Some brewers keep a foot in by helping with recipe development or sensory panels. Ask about that when you negotiate the move.

If your brewery allows it, spend a few days riding along with the sales team. Join visits, listen to the conversations and notice how many doors close. Offer to run a staff training session at an outlet. That gives you a real feel for the job without leaving the brewhouse.

Many hospitality people make the move from the other direction. Our guide on moving from hospitality to brewery sales shows what they bring that a brewer may need to learn.

Pick three outlets that pour your beer. Visit each on a quiet afternoon. Taste the beer from the tap and compare it with a sample straight from the brewery. Ask when the lines were last cleaned. Write down what you find. If you enjoyed those conversations and want more of them, sales may be your next move.
faqs: Is it a good idea for a brewer to move into sales?
It can be, if you enjoy people, travel and persistence. Brewers bring credibility and technical skill, but must learn targets, negotiation and outlet economics.
What advantage does a brewer have in beer sales?
Credibility and technical knowledge. A brewer can explain the beer, train staff and diagnose draught problems that would otherwise be blamed on the brewery.
Will I lose my brewing skills in sales?
Hands-on skills fade over time. Some brewers stay involved in recipe development or sensory panels to keep their hand in.
How can I test whether sales suits me?
Ride along with the sales team for a few days, join outlet visits and run a staff training session before you commit.
